Repeat the last change
rows.evidence: The dot command lets us repeat the last change. It is the most powerful and versatile command in Vim.

rows.meaning: Delete the character under the cursor
rows.evidence: The x command deletes the character under the cursor. When we use the dot command in this context, “repeat last change” tells Vim to delete the character under the cursor:

rows.meaning: Undo the last change (restore earlier state)
rows.evidence: We can restore the file to its original state by pressing the u key a few times to undo the changes.

rows.meaning: Delete the current line as a whole
rows.evidence: The dd command also performs a deletion, but this one acts on the current line as a whole.

rows.meaning: Increase indentation from the current line to end of file
rows.evidence: Finally, the >G command increases the indentation from the current line until the end of the file. If we follow this command with the dot command, then “repeat last change” tells Vim to increase the indentation level from the current position to the end of the file. In this example, we’ll start with the cursor on the second line to highlight the difference

rows.meaning: Move the cursor down one line
rows.evidence: But let’s take a closer look at this pattern: j$.. The j command moves the cursor down one line, and then the $ command moves it to the end of the line. We’ve used two keystrokes just to maneuver our cursor into position so that we can use the dot command. Do you sense that there’s room for improvement here?

rows.meaning: Append at the end of the current line (enters Insert mode)
rows.evidence: While the a command appends after the current cursor position, the A command appends at the end of the current line. It doesn’t matter where our cursor is at the time, pressing A will switch to Insert mode and move the cursor to the end of the line. In other words, it squashes $a into a single keystroke. In Two for the Price of One, we see that Vim has a handful of compound commands.

rows.meaning: Delete the character under the cursor and enter Insert mode
rows.evidence: The s command compounds two steps into one: it deletes the character under the cursor and then enters Insert mode. Having deleted the + sign, we then type + and leave Insert mode.

rows.meaning: Jump to the next occurrence of a character on the line
rows.evidence: There’s another trick in this example. The f{char} command tells Vim to look ahead for the next occurrence of the specified character and then move the cursor directly to it if a match is found (see fⓘ). So when we type f+, our cursor goes straight to the next + symbol. We’ll learn more about the f{char} command in Tip 50.

rows.meaning: Repeat the last f{char} search forward
rows.evidence: Having made our first change, we could jump to the next occurrence by repeating the f+ command, but there’s a better way. The ; command will repeat the last search that the f command performed. So instead of typing f+ four times, we can use that command once and then follow up by using the ; command three times.

rows.meaning: Repeat the last f{char} search in the reverse direction
rows.evidence: Whenever Vim makes it easy to repeat an action or a motion, it always provides some way of backing out in case we accidentally go too far. In the case of the dot command, we can always hit the u key to undo the last change. If we hit the ; key too many times after using the f{char} command, we’ll miss our mark. But we can back up again by pressing the , key, which repeats the last f{char} search in the reverse direction (see Tip 50).

rows.meaning: Substitute every occurrence of content with copy in the file
Search for the word under the cursor
rows.evidence: You might have guessed by now that the dot command is my favorite single-key Vim trigger. In second place is the * command. This executes a search for the word under the cursor at that moment (see *ⓘ).

rows.meaning: Jump to the next match of the current search
rows.evidence: Having executed a search for the word “content,” we can now advance to the next occurrence just by hitting the n key. In this case, pressing *nn would cycle through all matches, taking us back to where we started.

rows.meaning: Change to the end of the word, then enter Insert mode
rows.evidence: With our cursor positioned at the start of the word “content,” we are poised to change it. This involves two steps: deleting the word “content” and then typing its replacement. The cw command deletes to the end of the word and then drops us into Insert mode, where we can spell out the word “copy.” Vim records our keystrokes until we leave Insert mode, so the full sequence cwcopy<Esc> is considered to be a single change. Pressing the . command deletes to the end of the current word and changes it to “copy.”

rows.meaning: Undo the most recent change; each trip into Insert mode counts as one change.
rows.evidence: The u key triggers the undo command, which reverts the most recent change. A change could be anything that modifies the text in the document. That includes commands triggered from Normal, Visual, and Command-Line modes, but a change could also encompass any text entered (or deleted) in Insert mode. So we could also say that i{insert some text}<Esc> constitutes a change.

rows.meaning: Delete backward from the cursor to the start of the current word.
rows.evidence: Pressing db deletes from the cursor’s starting position to the beginning of the word, but it leaves the final “h” intact. We can delete this rogue character by pressing x. That gives us a Vim golf score of 3.

rows.meaning: Motion that moves the cursor backward to the start of the current word.
rows.evidence: We have to start by maneuvering our cursor into position with the b motion. Once it’s in place, we can excise the word with a single dw command. Once again, our Vim golf score is 3.

rows.meaning: Delete the single character under the cursor.
rows.evidence: The backward deletion technique involves two operations: db deletes to the start of the word and then x deletes a single character. If we invoke the dot command, it repeats the single character deletion (. == x). That’s not what I would call a big win.

rows.meaning: Delete from the cursor to the start of the next word.
rows.evidence: The forward deletion technique also involves two steps. This time, b is just a plain motion, while dw makes a change. The dot command repeats dw, deleting from the cursor position to the beginning of the next word. It so happens that we’re already at the end of the line. There is no “next word,” so in this context the dot command isn’t useful. But at least it’s shorthand for something longer (. == dw).

rows.meaning: Delete a whole word plus its surrounding whitespace (delete a word).
rows.evidence: The daw command is easily remembered by the mnemonic delete a word. We’ll go into more detail on text objects in Tip 52, and Tip 53.

rows.meaning: Dot command: repeat the last change, here repeating daw on another word.
rows.evidence: The final solution only invokes a single operation: daw. This technique doesn’t just remove the word, it also deletes a whitespace character. As a result, our cursor ends up on the last character of the word “is.” If we invoke the dot command, it will repeat the instruction to delete a word. This time, the dot command does something truly useful (. == daw).

rows.meaning: Increment the number at or after the cursor; a count adds that amount.
rows.evidence: The <C-a> and <C-x> commands perform addition and subtraction on numbers. When run without a count they increment by one, but if we prefix a number, then we can add or subtract by any whole number. For example, if we positioned our cursor on a 5 character, running 10<C-a> would modify it to read 15.

rows.meaning: Yank the current line and paste it below, duplicating the line.
rows.evidence: We’re going to duplicate the last line and make two small modifications to it: replace the word “blog” with “news,” and change “0px” to “-180px.” We can duplicate the line by running yyp and then using cW to change the first word. But how should we deal with that number?

rows.meaning: Decrement by 180; with the cursor off a digit it jumps forward to the first number on the line.
rows.evidence: One approach would be to jump to the digit with f0 and then dip into Insert mode to change the value by hand: i-18<Esc>. But it’s quicker just to run 180<C-x>. Since our cursor isn’t on a digit to begin with, it jumps forward to the first one that it finds. That saves us the step of moving the cursor by hand. Let’s see this work flow in action:

rows.meaning: Count applied to the delete operator, deleting two words (same result as d2w).
rows.evidence: We can approach this in a handful of ways. Both d2w and 2dw will work. With d2w, we invoke the delete command and then give 2w as the motion. We could read that as “delete two words.” However, 2dw turns things around. This time the count applies to the delete command, but the motion acts over a single word. We could read this as “delete a word two times.” Putting semantics aside, we get the same result either way.

rows.meaning: Change three words with a count, then type the replacement text.
Combine the gU operator with the aw text object to uppercase the current word.
rows.evidence: Suppose that we already know how to delete a word using daw, and then we learn about the gU command (see gUⓘ). It’s an operator too, so we can invoke gUaw to convert the current word to SHOUTY case. If we then expand our vocabulary to include the ap motion, which acts upon a paragraph, then we find two new operations at our disposal: dap to delete, or gUap to make the whole paragraph shout.

rows.meaning: Operator invoked in duplicate acts on the current line: delete the whole line.
rows.evidence: Vim’s grammar has just one more rule: when an operator command is invoked in duplicate, it acts upon the current line. So dd deletes the current line, while >> indents it. The gU command is a special case. We can make it act upon the current line by running either gUgU or the shorthand gUU.

rows.meaning: Jump to the top of the file with gg, then =G autoindents everything to the end.
rows.evidence: If we wanted to autoindent the entire file using the = command, we could run gg=G (that is, gg to jump to the top of the file and then =G to autoindent everything from the cursor position to the end of the file). But if we had the textobj-entire plugin installed, we could simply run =ae. It wouldn’t matter where our cursor was when we ran this command; it would always act upon the entire file.

rows.meaning: Delete back one character (backspace) while staying in Insert mode
Delete back one word
Delete back to start of line
Switch to Normal mode
Switch to Normal mode; synonymous with <Esc>
Switch to Insert Normal mode to run one Normal command, then return to Insert mode
Insert the contents of the named register at the cursor without leaving Insert mode
rows.evidence: The general format of the command is <C-r>{register}, where {register} is the address of the register we want to insert (see i_CTRL-Rⓘ).

rows.meaning: Insert register text literally and fix unintended indentation
rows.evidence: The <C-r><C-p>{register} command is smarter. It inserts text literally and fixes any unintended indentation (see i_CTRL-R_CTRL-Pⓘ). But it’s a bit of a handful! If I want to paste a register containing multiple lines of text, I prefer to switch to Normal mode and use one of the put commands (see Tip 63).

rows.meaning: Open the expression-register prompt from Insert mode; <CR> inserts the evaluated result
rows.evidence: The expression register is addressed by the = symbol. From Insert mode we can access it by typing <C-r>=. This opens a prompt at the bottom of the screen where we can type the expression that we want to evaluate. When done, we hit <CR>, and Vim inserts the result at our current position in the document.

rows.meaning: Insert an arbitrary character by its three-digit decimal code
rows.evidence: We can tell Vim to insert any arbitrary character if we know its numeric code. From Insert mode, we just have to type <C-v>{code}, where {code} is the address of the character that we want to insert.

rows.meaning: Insert a character by four-digit hexadecimal code, for example <C-v>u00bf for the inverted question mark
rows.evidence: But what if we wanted to insert a character whose numeric code is longer than three digits? For example, the Unicode Basic Multilingual Plane has an address space for up to 65,535 characters. It turns out that we can enter all of these using a four-digit hexadecimal code if we type <C-v>u{1234} (note the u preceding the digit this time). Let’s say we wanted to insert an inverted question mark symbol (“¿”), which is represented by the character code 00bf. From Insert mode, we would just have to type <C-v>u00bf. See i_CTRL-V_digitⓘ for more details.

rows.meaning: Insert the character represented by a two-character digraph, for example <C-k>?I
rows.evidence: Digraphs are easy to use. From Insert mode, we just type <C-k>{char1}{char2}. So if we wanted to insert the “¿” character, which is represented by the digraph ?I, we would simply type <C-k>?I.

rows.meaning: Enter Replace mode, which overwrites existing text until <Esc>
rows.evidence: From Normal mode, we can engage Replace mode with the R command. As the example demonstrates, typing “, b” overwrites the existing “. B” characters. And when we’re finished with Replace mode, we can hit the <Esc> key to return to Normal mode. Not all keyboards have an <Insert> key, but if yours does, then you can use it to toggle between Insert and Replace modes.

rows.meaning: Enter Virtual Replace mode, which overwrites screen columns and treats a tab as spaces
rows.evidence: Vim has a second variant of Replace mode. Virtual Replace mode is triggered with gR and treats the tab character as though it consisted of spaces. Suppose that we position the cursor on a tab stop spanning eight columns of screen real estate. If we switch to Virtual Replace mode, we could type up to seven characters, each of which would be inserted in front of the tab character. Finally, if we typed an eighth character, it would replace the tab stop.

rows.meaning: Single-shot replace: overwrite one character (or one virtual character) and return to Normal mode
rows.evidence: Vim also provides a single-shot version of Replace mode and Virtual Replace mode. The r{char} and gr{char} commands allow us to overwrite a single character before switching straight back to Normal mode (rⓘ).

rows.meaning: Enable character-wise Visual mode from Normal mode
rows.evidence: The v key is our gateway into Visual mode. From Normal mode, we can press v by itself to enable character-wise Visual mode. Line-wise Visual mode is enabled by pressing V (with the Shift key), and block-wise Visual mode by pressing <C-v> (with the Control key). These commands are summarized in the following table:

rows.meaning: Enable line-wise Visual mode (Shift-v)
Enable block-wise Visual mode (Ctrl-v)
Reselect the last visual selection, whatever its submode
rows.evidence: The gv command is a useful little shortcut. It reselects the range of text that was last selected in Visual mode. No matter whether the previous selection was character-wise, line-wise, or block-wise, the gv command should do the right thing. The only case where it might get confused is if the last selection has since been deleted.

rows.meaning: Switch to the other (free) end of the selection so its bounds can be redefined
rows.evidence: The range of a Visual mode selection is marked by two ends: one end is fixed and the other moves freely with our cursor. We can use the o key to toggle the free end. This is really handy if halfway through defining a selection we realize that we started in the wrong place. Rather than leaving Visual mode and starting afresh, we can just hit o and redefine the bounds of the selection. The following demonstrates how we can use this technique:

rows.meaning: Toggle between Visual and Select modes
rows.evidence: We can toggle between Visual and Select modes by pressing <C-g>. The only visible difference is the message at the bottom of screen, which switches between -- VISUAL -- and -- SELECT --. But if we type any printable character in Select mode, it will replace the selection and switch to Insert mode. Of course, from Visual mode you could just as well use the c key to change the selection.

rows.meaning: Visually select the word under the cursor
rows.evidence: Let’s revisit the simple example where we wanted to change the word “March” to “April.” This time, suppose that we have left the confines of the text area on a web page and we’re comfortably back inside Vim. We place our cursor somewhere on the word “March” and run viw to visually select the word. Now, we can’t just type the word “April” because that would trigger the A command and append the text “pril”! Instead, we’ll use the c command to change the selection, deleting the word and dropping us into Insert mode, where we can type out the word “April” in full. This pattern of usage is similar to our original example, except that we use the c key instead of backspace.

rows.meaning: Visually select the inner contents of the current tag (text object)
rows.evidence: We can select the inner contents of a tag by running vit, which can be read as: visually select inside the tag. The it command is a special kind of motion called a text object, which we’ll cover in detail in Tip 52.

rows.meaning: Convert the selected characters to uppercase
rows.evidence: In Visual mode, we make a selection and then act on it. In this case, we could use the U command, which converts the selected characters to uppercase (v_Uⓘ). See Table 4, Uppercasing in Visual Mode.

rows.meaning: Normal-mode operator that uppercases the text covered by a motion
rows.evidence: The Visual mode U command has a Normal mode equivalent: gU{motion} (gUⓘ). If we use this to make the first change, we can complete the subsequent edits using the Dot Formula:

rows.meaning: Move down one line and repeat the last change with the dot command (Dot Formula)
rows.evidence: Running j. advances our cursor to the next line and then repeats the last change. It works fine on line two, but if we try it again we end up with this strange-looking result:

rows.meaning: Indent the selected range by one level
rows.evidence: In our malformed Python excerpt, the two lines below the while keyword should be indented further by two levels. We could fix it by visually selecting the text and triggering the > command to indent it. But that would only increase the indentation by one level before dropping us back into Normal mode.

rows.meaning: Delete the selected column in Visual-Block mode
rows.evidence: To begin, we use <C-v> to engage Visual-Block mode; then we define the column selection by moving our cursor down several lines. Pressing the x key deletes that column, and the dot command repeats the deletion for the same range of text. We repeat until the two columns are about the right distance apart.

rows.meaning: Replace every character in the selection with a pipe character
rows.evidence: Now that we’ve lined up the two columns of text where we want them, we’re ready to draw a line between them. We can reselect our last visual selection using the gv command and then press r| to replace each character in the selection with a pipe character.

rows.meaning: Append text at the end of each line of a Visual-Block selection
rows.evidence: Having defined our selection, we can append at the end of each line using the A command (see Vim’s Conventions for “i” and “a” Keys). This drops us into Insert mode on the topmost line of our selection. Anything that we type will appear on this line only for the duration of Insert mode, but as soon as we revert to Normal mode, our changes are propagated across the rest of the lines that we selected.

rows.meaning: Print lines 2 through 5, using line-number addresses for the range.
Replace the first occurrence of Practical with Pragmatic on every line of the file.
Print the lines covered by the most recent Visual-mode selection.
Print the range from the opening <html> tag to the closing </html> tag, using pattern addresses.
Print that same block without its first and last lines, using offset addresses.
Duplicate the current line below itself without using a register.
Append a semicolon at the end of every line by running a Normal mode command across a range.
Repeat the most recently executed Ex command.
rows.evidence: In Chapter 1, The Vim Way, we saw how the . command can be used to repeat the last change. But the dot command won’t replay changes made from Vim’s command line. Instead, we can repeat the last Ex command by pressing @: (see @:ⓘ).

rows.meaning: Reveal the list of possible tab-completions for the col prefix.
Insert the word under the cursor at the command-line prompt.
rows.evidence: At Vim’s command line, the <C-r><C-w> mapping copies the word under the cursor and inserts it at the command-line prompt. We can use this to save ourselves a bit of typing.

rows.meaning: Open the command-line window with the history of Ex commands.
rows.evidence: Each of these commands is already in our history, so we shouldn’t have to type the entire command line from scratch. But how can we merge two records from our history into one? Press q: and meet the command-line window (see cmdwinⓘ).

rows.meaning: Run an external command, with % standing for the current file name.
Filter lines 2 through the last line through the external sort command.
Run :join on every line where href matches (global command).
Source the script once in every file of the argument list.
List all loaded buffers with their numbers and status flags.
Switch to the next buffer in the buffer list.
Toggle between the current buffer and the alternate file.
rows.evidence: The % symbol indicates which of the buffers is visible in the current window, while the # symbol represents the alternate file. We can quickly toggle between the current and alternate files by pressing <C-^>. Press it once, and we’ll switch to a.txt; press it a second time, and we’ll get back to b.txt.

rows.meaning: Jump directly to a buffer by number, or by a unique fragment of its name.
rows.evidence: The :ls listing starts with a digit, which is assigned to each buffer automatically on creation. We can jump directly to a buffer by number, using the :buffer N command (see :bⓘ). Alternatively, we can use the more intuitive form, :buffer {bufname}. The {bufname} need only contain enough characters from the filepath to uniquely identify the buffer. If we enter a string that matches more than one of the items in the buffer list, we can use tab-completion to choose between the options (see Tip 32).

rows.meaning: Remove buffers from the buffer list without touching their files on disk.
Print the current contents of the argument list.
Replace the argument list with the given filenames, wildcards, or shell output.
Populate the argument list from several globs at once.
Populate the argument list from the output of a shell command.
Force a switch to the next buffer, abandoning unsaved changes.
Execute an Ex command on each file in the argument list.
Split the current window horizontally or vertically, reusing the current buffer.
rows.evidence: When Vim starts up, it contains a single window. We can divide this window horizontally with the <C-w>s command, which creates two windows of equal height. Or we can use the <C-w>v command to split the window vertically, producing two windows of equal width. We can repeat these commands as often as we like, splitting our workspace again and again in a process that resembles cell division.

rows.meaning: Cycle the focus between open windows.
Open a file in a new tab page.
rows.evidence: We can open a new tab page with the :tabedit {filename} command. If we omit the {filename} argument, then Vim creates a new tab page containing an empty buffer.

rows.meaning: Jump to tab page N, or move to the next/previous tab.
rows.evidence: Tabs are numbered starting from 1. We can switch between tabs with the {N}gt command, which can be remembered as goto tab {N}. When this command is prefixed with a number, Vim jumps to the specified tab, but if the number is omitted, Vim advances to the next tab. The gT command does the same but in reverse.

rows.meaning: Open a file from a path relative to Vim's working directory.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Expand the active buffer's filepath on the command line.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Expand the active buffer's directory using the :h modifier.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Open a sibling file by expanding the active directory, then tab-completing the name.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Add the app/ tree to the 'path' search list.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Open a file by name, searching the directories in 'path'.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Open netrw's file explorer for the current working directory.
rows.evidence: We can open the file explorer window with the :edit {path} command by supplying a directory name (instead of a filename) as the {path} argument. The dot symbol stands for the current working directory, so if we run the :edit . command, we can bring up a file explorer for the project root.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Open netrw's file explorer for the directory of the active buffer.
rows.evidence: If we wanted to open a file explorer for the directory of the current file, we could do so by typing :edit %:h (see Open a File Relative to the Active File Directory, for an explanation). But the netrw plugin provides a more convenient way with the :Explore command (see :Exploreⓘ).
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Open netrw's file explorer in a horizontal or vertical split window.
rows.evidence: In addition to :Explore, netrw also provides :Sexplore and :Vexplore commands, which open the file explorer in a horizontal split window or vertical split window, respectively.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Switch back to the buffer that was previously displayed.
rows.evidence: Think of each window as a playing card. One side of the card shows the contents of a file, and the other side shows the file explorer. When we run the :Explore command, the card for the active window flips over to show the side with the file explorer (frame 2 of the figure). After choosing the file we want to edit, we press <CR> and the card flips over again, this time showing the contents of the file that we just selected (frame 3 of the figure). After summoning the file explorer view, if we decide that we want to switch back to the buffer we were already editing, we can do so using the <C-^> command.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Echo the name and status of the current file.
rows.evidence: The :edit {file} command is most commonly used to open a file that already exists. But if we specify a filepath that doesn’t correspond to an existing file, then Vim will create a new empty buffer. If we press <C-g>, we’ll see that the buffer is labeled as “new file” (the <C-g> command echoes the name and status of the current file; see ctrl-Gⓘ). When we run the :write command, Vim will attempt to write the contents of that buffer to a new file using the filepath that was specified when the buffer was created.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Write the buffer's contents to its file on disk.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Create the buffer's missing parent directories with the external mkdir program.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Force a write, overriding the 'readonly' option.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Pipe the buffer through sudo tee to overwrite a root-owned file.
rows.chapterTitle: Open Files and Save Them to Disk

rows.meaning: Move left, down, up, or right one step without leaving the home row
rows.evidence: Just as with any other text editor, Vim lets us use the arrow keys to move the cursor around, but it also provides an alternative by way of the h, j, k, and l keys. They work as follows:

rows.meaning: Move down or up by display line rather than by real line
rows.evidence: Understanding the difference between real and display lines is important because Vim provides motions for interacting with both kinds. The j and k commands move down and up by real lines, whereas the gj and gk commands move down and up by display lines.

rows.meaning: Jump to the first character or the end of a real line; g-prefixed forms act on display lines
rows.evidence: Note the pattern: j, k, 0, and $ all interact with real lines, while prefixing any of these with g tells Vim to act on display lines instead.

rows.meaning: Move word-wise to the next/previous word start or word end
rows.evidence: We can think of these motions as coming in pairs: the w and b commands both target the start of a word, while the e and ge commands target the end of a word. w and e both advance the cursor forward, while b and ge move the cursor backward. This matrix of word-wise motions is illustrated here:

rows.meaning: WORD-wise versions of w, b, e, and ge
rows.evidence: We’ve been talking a lot about words, but so far we haven’t pinned down what a word actually is. Vim provides two definitions and distinguishes between them by calling one a “word” and the other a “WORD.” Each word-wise motion we met earlier has a WORD-wise equivalent, including W, B, E, and gE.

rows.meaning: Search forward to a character, repeat that search, and reverse it
rows.evidence: The f{char}, ;, and , commands are part of a set of character-search commands. This table lists them all:

rows.meaning: Search till just before/after the target character
rows.evidence: Think of the t{char} and T{char} commands as searching till the specified character. The cursor stops one character before {char}, whereas the f{char} and F{char} commands position the cursor on top of the specified character.

rows.meaning: Search forward for a multi-character pattern
rows.evidence: We could do so by searching for the word: /takes<CR>. It only occurs once in this short sample, so that would be sure to get us where we want to go in a single move. But let’s see if we can we do it with even fewer keystrokes:

rows.meaning: Repeat the last search forward or backward
rows.evidence: Even if we had searched for the two-letter “ta” fragment and ended up in the wrong place, we could jump to the next occurrence by repeating the previous search with the n command. Also, if we pressed the n key too many times, we could back up again with the N command. The mantra from Tip 4, should be becoming familiar by now: act, repeat, reverse.

rows.meaning: Delete up to a search match, using the search as an exclusive motion
Visually select everything inside a pair of braces
rows.evidence: Suppose that our cursor was positioned inside a set of curly braces and we wanted to visually select the text inside the {}. Press vi}:

rows.meaning: Change the text inside double quotes
rows.evidence: We can read the ci" command as “change inside the double quotes.” The cit command can be read as “change inside the tag.” We could just as easily use the yit command to yank the text from inside the tag, or dit to delete it.

rows.meaning: Delete the current word with the aw text object
rows.evidence: Suppose that we want to delete the word “excellent” from the following sentence. We can do it using the daw command:

rows.meaning: Set mark m and jump back to it
rows.evidence: The mm and `m commands make a handy pair. Respectively, they set the mark m and jump to it. Swap Two Words, shows one example of how they can be used for a quick mark-then-snap-back maneuver.

rows.meaning: Jump between matching parentheses, braces, or brackets
rows.evidence: The % command lets us jump between opening and closing sets of parentheses (see %ⓘ). It works with (), {}, and [], as this example demonstrates:

rows.meaning: Jump backward through the jump list, like a browser's back button
rows.evidence: In web browsers, we’re used to using the back button to return to pages that we visited earlier. Vim provides a similar feature by way of the jump list: the <C-o> command is like the back button, while the complementary <C-i> command is like the forward button. These commands allow us to traverse Vim’s jump list, but what exactly is a jump?

rows.meaning: Jump forward through the jump list, like a browser's forward button
rows.evidence: In web browsers, we’re used to using the back button to return to pages that we visited earlier. Vim provides a similar feature by way of the jump list: the <C-o> command is like the back button, while the complementary <C-i> command is like the forward button. These commands allow us to traverse Vim’s jump list, but what exactly is a jump?

rows.meaning: Print the contents of the jump list
Jump directly to a line number; this counts as a jump
Search forward and jump to the next occurrence of the pattern
Jump to the next or previous search match
Jump to the matching parenthesis
Jump to the start of the previous or next sentence
Jump to the start of the previous or next paragraph
Jump to the file name under the cursor
Jump to the definition of the keyword under the cursor
Traverse backward or forward through the change list
rows.evidence: This example output shows that Vim records the line and column number for each change. Using the g; and g, commands, we can traverse backward and forward through the change list. As a memory aid for g; and g,, it may help to remember that the ; and , commands can be used to repeat or reverse the f{char} command (see Tip 50).

rows.meaning: Restore the cursor to the last insertion point and switch back to Insert mode
rows.evidence: The `^ mark references the last insertion, which is slightly more specific than the last change. If we leave Insert mode and then scroll around the document, we can quickly carry on where we left off by pressing gi (giⓘ). In a single move, that uses the `^ mark to restore the cursor position and then switches back into Insert mode. It’s a great little time saver!

rows.meaning: Create a mark at the cursor; uppercase letters create global marks
rows.evidence: The m{letter} command allows us to create a mark at the current cursor position (mⓘ). Lowercase letters create marks that are local to a buffer, whereas uppercase letters create global marks. Having set a mark, we can snap our cursor back to it with the `{letter} command (`ⓘ).

rows.meaning: Snap the cursor back to a mark
rows.evidence: The m{letter} command allows us to create a mark at the current cursor position (mⓘ). Lowercase letters create marks that are local to a buffer, whereas uppercase letters create global marks. Having set a mark, we can snap our cursor back to it with the `{letter} command (`ⓘ).

rows.meaning: Cut the character under the cursor and put it after the cursor, transposing the next two characters
rows.evidence: Taken together, the xp commands can be considered as “Transpose the next two characters.”

rows.meaning: Cut the current line and put it below its successor, transposing the order of two lines
rows.evidence: The ddp sequence could be considered to stand for “Transpose the order of this line and its successor.”

rows.meaning: Yank the current line and put it below itself, duplicating the line as a template
rows.evidence: Note the similarities between these two sequences, ddp and yyp. The first does a line-wise cut and paste, which effectively transposes the order of two lines. The second sequence does a line-wise copy and paste, which effectively duplicates a line.

rows.meaning: Yank the current word into the unnamed register
rows.evidence: To begin with, our cursor is already on the word we want to copy, so we can get it into the unnamed register by typing yiw.

rows.meaning: Delete (cut) the current word, which also overwrites the unnamed register
rows.evidence: Next we move our cursor to the place where we want to paste our collection, but before we can put it there we’ll have to clear a space for it. So we run diw to delete the word somethingInTheWay.

rows.meaning: Put the register contents in front of the cursor
rows.evidence: Now we can hit the P key to paste the contents of our unnamed register in front of the cursor. But instead of pasting the word collection, which we yanked earlier, we get the word somethingInTheWay. What’s going on?

rows.meaning: Yank the current word into named register a
rows.evidence: For example, if we wanted to yank the current word into register a, we could run "ayiw. Or if we wanted to cut the current line into register b, we could run "bdd. Then we could paste the word from register a by typing "ap, or we could paste the line from register b by typing "bp.

rows.meaning: Put from the yank register, which a delete does not overwrite
rows.evidence: The diw command still overwrites the unnamed register, but it leaves the yank register untouched. We can safely paste from the yank register by pressing "0P, and Vim gives us the text that we want.

rows.meaning: Delete text into the black hole register, copying it nowhere
rows.evidence: The black hole register is a place from which nothing returns. It’s addressed by the underscore symbol (see quote_ⓘ). If we run the command "_d{motion}, then Vim deletes the specified text without saving a copy of it. This can be useful if we want to delete text without overwriting the contents of the unnamed register.

rows.meaning: Paste the contents of the system clipboard (plus) register
rows.evidence: If we use the cut or copy command to capture text in an external application, then we can paste it inside Vim using "+p command (or <C-r>+ from the Insert mode). Conversely, if we prefix Vim’s yank or delete commands with "+, the specified text will be captured in the system clipboard. That means we can easily paste it inside other applications.

rows.meaning: Used from Visual mode, replace the selection with the register contents (and swap the old selection into the register)
rows.evidence: When we use the p command in Visual mode, Vim replaces the selection with the contents of the specified register (see v_pⓘ). We can exploit this feature to solve our problem from Oops! I Clobbered My Yank:

rows.meaning: Insert a register's contents from Insert mode, always in front of the cursor
rows.evidence: I don’t like having to think about whether a character-wise region of text needs to go in front of the cursor or after it. For that reason, I sometimes prefer to paste character-wise regions of text from Insert mode using the <C-r>{register} mapping rather than using the Normal mode p and P commands. Using this technique, the text from the register is always inserted in front of the cursor position, just as though we were typing it in Insert mode.

rows.meaning: Put a line-wise register above the current line and leave the cursor at the end of the pasted text
rows.evidence: It’s worth noting that Vim also provides gp and gP commands. These also put the text before or after the current line, but they leave the cursor positioned at the end of the pasted text instead of at the beginning. The gP command is especially useful when duplicating a range of lines, as demonstrated here:

rows.meaning: Toggle the 'paste' option (used to switch it off again after pasting)
rows.evidence: When we’re finished using the system paste command, we should disable the ‘paste’ option again. That means switching back to Normal mode and then running the Ex command :set paste!. Don’t you think it would be handy if there were a way of toggling this option without leaving Insert mode?

rows.meaning: Assign <f5> to toggle the 'paste' option on and off
Begin recording keystrokes into the named register
rows.evidence: The q key functions both as the “record” button and the “stop” button. To begin recording our keystrokes, we type q{register}, giving the address of the register where we want to save the macro. We can tell that we’ve done it right if the word “recording” appears in the status line. Every command that we execute will be captured, right up until we press q again to stop recording.

rows.meaning: Stop recording the macro
rows.evidence: Pressing qa begins recording and saves our macro into register a. We then perform two changes on the first line: appending a semicolon and prepending the word var. Having completed both of those changes, we press q to stop recording our macro (qⓘ).

rows.meaning: Execute the macro stored in the named register
rows.evidence: The @{register} command executes the contents of the specified register (see @ⓘ). We can also use @@, which repeats the macro that was invoked most recently.

rows.meaning: Repeat the macro most recently invoked
rows.evidence: The @{register} command executes the contents of the specified register (see @ⓘ). We can also use @@, which repeats the macro that was invoked most recently.

rows.meaning: Play the macro in register a with a count, repeating it ten times
rows.evidence: Suppose that the macro was stored in the a register. Rather than executing @a ten times, we could prefix it with a count: 10@a. The beauty of this technique is that we can be unscrupulous about how many times we execute this macro. Don’t care for counting? It doesn’t matter! We could execute 100@a or even 1000@a, and it would produce the same result.

rows.meaning: Record a one-off macro in register q that runs ; then .
rows.evidence: We can simulate this by recording one of the simplest possible macros: qq;.q. Here, qq tells Vim to record the following keystrokes and save them to the q register. Then we type our commands ;. and finish recording the macro by pressing q one final time. Now we can execute the macro with a count: 11@q. This executes ;. eleven times.

rows.meaning: Append keystrokes to the existing macro in register a instead of overwriting it
rows.evidence: If we type qa, then Vim will record our keystrokes, saving them into register a by overwriting the existing contents of that register. If we type qA, then Vim will append our keystrokes to the existing contents of register a.

rows.meaning: Inspect the contents of register a
Run the macro once on each line of the selected range
rows.evidence: The :normal @a command tells Vim to execute the macro once for each line in the selection. Just as before, the macro succeeds on the first two lines and then aborts on line three, but it doesn’t stall there this time—it completes the job. Why?

rows.meaning: Run the macro once in every buffer in the argument list
Advance to the next file in the argument list; failure on the last file aborts a series macro
rows.evidence: While we could run 3@a to execute the macro on each of the remaining files in the buffer list, there’s no need to be so precise about it. When we reach the last buffer in the argument list, the :next command fails and the macro aborts. So, rather than specifying an exact count, we only have to ensure that we provide a number that’s large enough: 22 will do, and it’s easy to type.

rows.meaning: Increment the counter variable i
Paste the contents of register a below the current line as plain text
Yank from the cursor to the end of the line into register a, character-wise
rows.evidence: When we run the command 0 followed by "ay$, we yank every character on that line except for the carriage return. Having captured everything that we want to keep into register a, we can then run dd to delete the line. This will end up in the default register, but we won’t use it.

rows.meaning: Insert the value of variable i via the expression register in Insert mode
rows.evidence: The :echo command is fine for revealing the value that is assigned to a variable, but ideally we want to insert that value into the document. We can do that using the expression register. In Tip 16, we saw that the expression register can be used to do simple sums and to insert the result into the document. We can insert the value stored in variable i just by running <C-r>=i<CR> in Insert mode.

rows.meaning: Enable case-insensitive search globally.
Override case sensitivity for one search: \c ignores case, \C forces it.
rows.evidence: We can override Vim’s default case sensitivity using the \c and \C items. Lowercase \c causes the search pattern to ignore case, while the uppercase \C item forces case sensitivity. If either of these items is used in a search pattern, the value of ‘ignorecase’ is overridden for that search.

rows.meaning: Magic-search regex matching three- or six-digit hex colors.
Very magic hex-color regex using the \x character class.
Very nomagic search for the literal text a.k.a.
Match a repeated word with a capture group and \1 backreference.
Group alternatives without capturing the submatch.
Substitute using the last search and captured first/last names.
Search for the whole word 'the' using word boundaries.
rows.evidence: If we specifically want to match “the” as a word rather than a fragment, we can use word boundary delimiters. In very magic searches, these are represented by the < and > symbols. So if we amended our search to /\v<the><CR>, it would find only one match in the excerpt.

rows.meaning: Search forward or backward for the word under the cursor.
rows.evidence: Even if we don’t make a habit of using the word boundary items when composing our own search patterns, we use them indirectly each time we trigger the * or # commands (see *ⓘ). These search forward and backward, respectively, for the word under the cursor. If we examine the search history after using either of these commands (by pressing /<Up>), we’ll see that the last search pattern is wrapped with word delimiters. Incidentally, the g* and g# variants perform the same searches without word delimiters.

rows.meaning: Positive-lookaround rewrite of the quoted-text pattern.
Crop the match to the quoted contents with \zs and \ze.
Yank the bracketed URL into register u.
rows.evidence: With our cursor placed anywhere inside the brackets, we can yank the URL into register u with the command "uyi[ (mnemonic: u stands for URL). We then type /\V<C-r>u<CR> to populate the search field with the contents of that same register. Our search prompt looks like this:

rows.meaning: Insert register u into the search prompt.
rows.evidence: With our cursor placed anywhere inside the brackets, we can yank the URL into register u with the command "uyi[ (mnemonic: u stands for URL). We then type /\V<C-r>u<CR> to populate the search field with the contents of that same register. Our search prompt looks like this:

rows.meaning: Escape / and \ in a very nomagic search to match the full URL literally.
Open the forward search prompt; enter a pattern, then press <CR> to execute the search
rows.evidence: From Normal mode, the / key brings up Vim’s search prompt. Here we can enter the pattern, or literal text, that we want to search for. Vim does nothing until we press the <CR> key to execute the search. If we press the <Esc> key instead, the search prompt will be dismissed and we’ll return to Normal mode.

rows.meaning: Open the search prompt so that Vim scans backward through the document
rows.evidence: When a search is initiated with the / key, Vim scans the document forward. If we use the ? key to bring up the search prompt, Vim searches backward instead. The search prompt always begins with either the / or ? character, which indicates in what direction the search will scan.

rows.meaning: Jump to the next match or the previous match for the current search pattern
rows.evidence: The n command jumps to the next match, and the N command jumps to the previous match. We can easily navigate between matches in the current document with the n and N commands. But the definition of “next match” depends on context.

rows.meaning: Move to the next match, then enable Visual mode and select the matching text (also usable as an operator motion)
rows.evidence: When used from Normal mode, gn moves the cursor to the next match, then enables Visual mode and selects the matching text. If your cursor is already on a match, then gn will select the current match without you having to move the cursor. We’ll look at this command in in more detail in Tip 84.

rows.meaning: Mute search highlighting temporarily; it stays muted until the next new or repeat search
rows.evidence: Vim has a more elegant solution. The :nohlsearch command can be used to mute the search highlighting temporarily (see :nohⓘ). It will stay muted until the next time you execute a new or repeat search command. See Create a Shortcut to Mute Highlighting, for a suggested mapping.

rows.meaning: Mapping that clears the screen and mutes search highlighting
Option that previews the first match while the search pattern is still being typed
rows.evidence: By default, Vim sits idle as we prepare our search pattern, only springing into action when we press <CR>. My favorite enhancement is enabled with the ‘incsearch’ setting (see 'incsearch'ⓘ). This tells Vim to show a preview of the first match based on what has been entered so far into the search field. Each time we enter another character, Vim instantly updates the preview. This table illustrates how it works:

rows.meaning: Autocomplete the search field using the remainder of the current preview match
rows.evidence: Of course, we could simply type out the “carrot” in full. But here’s a handy shortcut: <C-r><C-w>. This autocompletes the search field using the remainder of the current preview match. If we used this command after entering “carr” into the search field, it would append “ot,” causing the match to encompass the entire word “carrot.”

rows.meaning: Search for lang and use the e offset to place the cursor at the end of the match
Repeat the previous search with an offset, reusing the pattern because the search field is left blank
rows.evidence: In the real world, it won’t always be obvious when a search offset will come in handy. Suppose that we started off by executing the search command without the offset. Then, after pressing n a couple of times, we realize that we’d prefer to place the cursor at the end of the match. That’s no problem: we could simply run //e<CR>. When we leave the search field blank like this, Vim reuses the pattern from the previous search. So this repeats the last search but with an offset.

rows.meaning: Uppercase the next search match by combining the gU operator with the gn motion
rows.evidence: The gUgn command transforms the matching text to uppercase.

rows.meaning: Open the command-line window prepopulated with search history, so patterns can be edited with modal editing
rows.evidence: Instead of pressing /<Up> to prefill the search field with our last pattern, let’s press q/ to summon the command-line window. This acts more or less like a regular Vim buffer, but it’s prepopulated with our search history, one item per line (see Meet the Command-Line Window). We can use the full power of Vim’s modal editing to amend the last pattern.

rows.meaning: Count the matches for the current pattern: the substitute n flag reports the count instead of replacing
Populate the quickfix list with every match of the current pattern in the current file
Redefine * in Visual mode to search for the current selection rather than the word under the cursor
Substitute the first match of going with rolling on the current line.
Add the g flag to change every match of going on the current line.
Prefix % to run the substitution on every line of the file.
Add the c flag to confirm or reject each match interactively.
Insert the contents of register 0 into the replacement field by value.
Evaluate the @0 register reference at run time, passing the register by reference.
Longhand for g&: repeat the last substitute with its replacement and flags across the whole file.
Repeat the last substitute reusing its flags, optionally with a new range.
rows.evidence: The :&& command requires some explanation, since the first and second & symbols have different meanings. The first one forms the :& Ex command, which repeats the last :substitute command (see :&ⓘ), while the second one indicates that the flags from the previous :s command should be reused.

rows.meaning: Very-magic pattern capturing three comma-separated fields as submatches.
Reorder the captured fields using backreferences in the replacement field.
Evaluate submatch(0)-1 to decrement each matched numeral.
Use an inline dictionary keyed by the captured word to swap words in one pass.
Match Pragmatic only when followed by Vim by ending the match with \ze.
Search the project for the last pattern and populate the quickfix list.
Run the substitute command on every file in the quickfix list, confirming each match.
Syntax template for the :global command
Run [cmd] on each line that does NOT match the pattern
rows.evidence: We can invert the behavior of the :global command either by running :global! or :vglobal (mnemonic: invert). Each of these tells Vim to execute [cmd] on each line that doesn’t match the specified pattern. In the next tip, we’ll see examples of both :global and :vglobal in action.

rows.meaning: Abbreviated global command: pattern, then :print — origin of “grep”
Search with a very magic pattern matching HTML tags
Delete every line matching the last search pattern

rows.meaning: Complete keywords using only the current buffer.
rows.evidence: The simplest mechanism for populating the autocomplete word list would be to use words only from the current buffer. Current file keyword completion does just that and is triggered with <C-x><C-n> (see compl-currentⓘ). This can be useful when generic keyword completion generates too many suggestions and you know that the word you want is somewhere in the current buffer.

rows.meaning: Complete keywords sourced from files included by the current file.
rows.evidence: Most programming languages provide some way of loading code from an external file or library. In C, this can be done using the #include directive, whereas Python uses import and Ruby uses require. If we are working on a file that includes code from another library, then it would be useful if Vim could read the contents of those referenced files when building a word list for autocompletion. And that is exactly what happens when we trigger keyword completion with the <C-x><C-i> command (see compl-keywordⓘ).

rows.meaning: Complete keywords sourced from the tags file.
rows.evidence: The main reason for indexing a codebase with ctags is to make it easier to navigate, but a tags file creates a useful by-product: a list of keywords that can be used for autocompletion. We can dial up this list using the <C-x><C-]> command (see compl-tagⓘ).

rows.meaning: Complete a word by dictionary lookup.

rows.evidence: Here’s one of my favorite tricks when working with the autocomplete pop-up menu. Try pressing <C-n><C-p>. That’s two separate commands: <C-n> followed immediately by <C-p> (although <C-p><C-n> would work just as well). The first command invokes autocomplete, summons the pop-up menu, and selects the first item in the word list. The second command selects the previous item in the word list, taking us back to where we started but without dismissing the pop-up menu. Now we can continue to type, and Vim will filter the word list in real time.
